(i) Explain the concept of a subgraph and determine how many distinct subgraphs can be formed from G, including itself and the null graph. (ii) Construct the complement graph of G and explain whether it is possible for both G and its complement to have exactly one vertex with an odd degree. Justify your answer.

(iii) Demonstrate another spanning tree S for the same graph G, different from T, and compute its total weight. Compare the weights of T and S to determine which one is minimal.

Analyze how the Dijkstra’s algorithm can be applied to find the shortest path between two vertices in a weighted graph, using the following scenario: A city planner needs to determine the most efficient route for a new bus line connecting two districts (vertex 𝑠 and vertex 𝑡) through several intermediate stations. The weighted edges represent the distances (in kilometers) between these stations. Describe step-by-step how Dijkstra’s algorithm can be implemented in this context, and calculate the shortest path length. Additionally, discuss any limitations of Dijkstra's algorithm in this application.

If such a graph can be constructed, provide an example of its structure. (ii) Construct the complement graph G' of G if it exists. Calculate the number of edges in both G and G'. (iii) Demonstrate how to convert this problem into a decision problem by asking: Does there exist a subgraph H of G such that H has exactly 5 vertices with odd degrees? If yes, describe one possible configuration for H.

Analyze and compare the properties of a complete graph and its complement, specifically focusing on their edge count, number of vertices, and connected components. Also, provide an example to illustrate your findings.

Analyze how the concept of Eulerian paths can be applied to solve real-world network design problems. Specifically, consider a scenario where a city planner needs to design a network for garbage collection in a small town with several streets forming a connected graph. The planner wants to ensure that a single garbage truck can travel each street exactly once and return to the starting point without any unvisited streets. (i) Construct an Eulerian graph representing the street layout of this town, ensuring it has at least 8 vertices. (ii) Determine if the constructed graph is Eulerian or semi-Eulerian. A small town has four main locations: a school, hospital, post office, and park. Each location is connected by roads to some or all other locations as follows: (i) The school is directly connected to the hospital but not to the post office. (ii) The hospital is connected to both the post office and the park. (iii) The post office is only connected to the hospital and the park. (iv) The park has no direct road connections to any other location. Construct a graph representing this network of roads using vertices for locations and edges for roads, ensuring that all given conditions are satisfied. (i) Determine the number of edges in this graph. (ii) Find the complement of this graph and describe its properties. (iii) Discuss whether it is possible to add one more road such that every location is directly connected to each other through a single road or through existing roads, without violating any given conditions.

(ii) Investigate whether the statement 'Among any three consecutive integers, at least one of them will have a divisor greater than 2' is always true, sometimes true, or never true. Analyze and prove using logical arguments: (i) If is an even integer, then its square is also an even integer. (ii) Investigate whether the statement ‘If a number is divisible by 4, then it is necessarily even’ can be logically derived from the first statement without additional assumptions.

Discuss the concept of equivalence relations and provide an example where the equivalence classes are finite. Additionally, explain how to use a directed graph to determine if a relation is reflexive and symmetric. Finally, illustrate these concepts using a specific set and relation.

Using propositional logic, solve the following problem: (i) Construct a truth table for the compound proposition Σ = (P → Q) ∧ (¬P ⇒ R). (ii) Determine whether the statement 'If P is true and Q is false, then R must be true' can be derived from the given compound proposition. Justify your answer by referring to specific rows in your truth table. (iii) Using your truth table, show that the statement Σ is logically equivalent to ((P ⇒ Q) ∧ (¬P)) → R. Demonstrate this by proving the biconditional relationship using truth table methods.
Demonstrate that for all real numbers x and y, if x ≤ y and y is an integer, then ⌊x⌋ ≤ y. Furthermore, prove by contradiction that there does not exist any real number z such that ⌊z⌋ > 2z + 1.

Analyze how a given symmetric matrix can be decomposed into the sum of two matrices that are not necessarily symmetric, using the concept of strong induction. Specifically, (i) construct a proof by strong induction for the claim; (ii) apply your proof to demonstrate the decomposition for a 3x3 symmetric matrix with all diagonal elements as 1 and non-diagonal elements as -1.

Discuss the pigeonhole principle and use it to solve the following problems. For each problem, state clearly how you apply the pigeonhole principle in your solution. (i) Show that among any 10 positive integers, there must be at least two whose difference is a multiple of 9. (ii) Prove that in any set of five distinct positive integers, there exist at least two numbers whose sum is a multiple of 8. (iii) A group consists of 23 people. Explain why it is necessary to have at least 3 people sharing the same birthday (ignoring leap years), and apply the pigeonhole principle to support your argument.

A library has 10 different books of various genres. (i) How many ways can a student choose 3 books such that at least one book is from the mystery genre? Assume 2 out of the 10 books are mysteries. (ii) In how many ways can the student select 5 books if they must include both a mystery and a science fiction book, given there is only 1 mystery and 1 science fiction book in the library?

A university mathematics club has 10 members (5 males and 5 females). The club decides to form a team of 4 members for an upcoming competition. (i) In how many ways can this be done if at least one female must be included in the team? (ii) If the team is chosen randomly, what is the probability that exactly two males are selected?

Consider the statement: For all real numbers and , if and only if . Using this information, (i) prove that if is an integer, then is also an integer; (ii) show that there exists a unique real number such that for any real number ; (iii) reformulate the following argument using predicate logic: 'For every integer , is even if and only if is odd', and determine its validity.
Analyze and prove, using propositional logic, that for any real numbers and , if then . Provide at least two different methods of proof.

Analyze the properties of the relation R defined by R = {(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2), (3, 4)} on the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Determine whether R is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and an equivalence relation. Justify your answers by applying the rules of propositional logic.
Analyze the statement 'For every even number n, n+2 is also an even number' using propositional calculus and determine its validity.
Analyze the statement 'For every prime number p greater than 2, p+2 is also a prime number' by constructing a truth table for its symbolic representation.
Examine and differentiate between a symmetric relation and an antisymmetric relation using examples on finite sets.
Demonstrate that for any real number x, if x is an integer, then the sum of x and 2 is also an integer.

Discuss the concept of a valid argument in formal logic by constructing a truth table for the following statement: 'If it is raining, then the ground is wet' and interpreting its validity.
Describe the process of determining whether a given argument is valid using predicate calculus. Provide an example to illustrate your explanation.
Demonstrate using formal logic that for every positive integer n, if n is odd then 2n + 1 is also an odd number.
Analyze the statement 'For every odd positive integer n, n^2 + 1 is also an even number.' and provide a proof or counterexample.

Examine and differentiate between a symmetric matrix and an anti-symmetric matrix using examples from 2x2 matrices. Also, prove that any square matrix can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric and an anti-symmetric matrix.
Examine and explain why the statement 'For every real number x, if x is rational then x^2 is also rational' is true or false using formal logic and provide a proof.

A relation R on a set A = {a, b, c, d} is defined as follows: R = {(a, a), (b, b), (c, c), (d, d), (a, b), (b, a), (b, c), (c, b)}. Determine whether the relation R is symmetric. If it is not symmetric, modify R to create a new relation S that is symmetric and demonstrate using formal logic that S satisfies the properties of symmetry. Additionally, represent both relations R and S as matrices.

Demonstrate that among any group of five distinct positive integers less than or equal to 10, there must be at least one pair whose difference is divisible by 3. Then, construct an example to show that this result does not hold for four such integers.

Construct a set A containing exactly 8 elements and define a relation R on A such that R contains at least 12 ordered pairs and demonstrate whether R is reflexive, symmetric, or transitive using a relation matrix. Additionally, apply the pigeonhole principle to explain why your constructed relation must have at least one pair (a, b) where aRb implies bRa, under certain conditions.

A library has 10 different books on mathematics and 10 different books on computer science. A student wants to select a collection of these books for her study. (i) In how many ways can she choose 3 books if at least one book must be from each subject? (ii) If the student decides to borrow exactly 4 books, in how many ways can this be done such that no more than two books are borrowed from any single subject?

Construct an elementary proof using strong induction to show that for any positive integer n, the number 7 divides at least one of the numbers in the sequence defined by a_1 = 2, and a_{n+1} = 3a_n + 4 for all n ≥ 1. Demonstrate your understanding by providing the base case, induction hypothesis, and inductive step clearly.

Construct a set A containing exactly 8 elements such that it forms an equivalence class under the relation R defined as follows: For any two elements x, y in A, (x, y) ∈ R if and only if x - y is divisible by 3. Demonstrate your construction using both set notation and a table showing all ordered pairs in R. Additionally, prove that R is an equivalence relation on the set A.

Discuss using a valid argument in formal logic why every odd positive integer can be expressed as 2k + 1 for some non-negative integer k, and then construct an elementary proof by strong induction to show that the sum of the first n odd positive integers is always a perfect square.

In a university department with 12 professors, each professor specializes in one of four subjects: Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, or Biology. (i) Describe how many ways can you select a committee of 4 professors if at least two must specialize in different subjects? (ii) Explain the principle used to calculate the number of ways to distribute 10 distinct research papers among these 12 professors such that no professor receives more than one paper.

Discuss using a valid argument in formal logic why for any set A with more than 4 elements, there must exist at least one subset of A containing exactly 3 elements such that their sum is even. Use the pigeonhole principle and concepts from permutations and combinations to explain your reasoning.

Analyze how many ways can 10 letters be distributed into 5 distinct mailboxes such that each mailbox receives at least one letter. Also, determine the number of ways to distribute these letters if no two consecutive letters are placed in the same mailbox. Provide a detailed explanation using appropriate counting principles and permutations.

Examine and analyze how the principles of propositional logic can be used to verify the validity of an argument in a real-world scenario involving conditional statements. Specifically, consider the following situation: A university library decides to implement a new policy where if a book is requested by at least 3 students on any given day (denoted as P), then it will be made available for immediate checkout (denoted as Q). Formulate this policy into a logical statement and use truth tables to determine under what conditions the policy will hold true. Discuss how this analysis can assist in decision-making processes within the library.

Determine whether the following statement is true or false: 'For every positive integer n, there exists a unique positive integer m such that 2m - 1 = n'. If the statement is true, provide a constructive proof to demonstrate its validity by formulating and interpreting logical statements. If the statement is false, construct a counterexample to disprove it.

Determine and construct an equivalence relation R on a finite set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} such that there are exactly two distinct equivalence classes. (ii) Draw the directed graph of the relation R to visually demonstrate its properties. (iii) Explain why your defined relation satisfies the conditions of an equivalence relation.

Determine whether the statement 'For all odd positive integers n, n^2 + 1 is even' is valid or not. Provide a proof for your answer.

Examine why the statement 'All positive integers that are not divisible by 4 differ in parity from their immediate predecessor' is true using induction. Provide a base case and an inductive step to prove this claim.
Analyze and differentiate between the statements 'For all real numbers x, if x^2 - 3x + 2 > 0' and 'There exists a real number x such that x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0', providing proofs for each.

Let 𝐴 = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Define a relation 𝑅 on 𝐴 as follows: 𝑅 = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (1,2), (2,1), (2,3), (3,2)}. (ii) Is 𝑅 symmetric? Explain. (iii) Is 𝑅 transitive? Explain. Determine how many positive integers less than or equal to 50 satisfy at least one of the following conditions: (i) are divisible by 3; (ii) are divisible by 4; and (iii) are not divisible by both 2 and 3. Construct a Venn diagram to illustrate your solution.

Determine the number of onto functions from a set A = {1, 2, 3, 4} to a set B = {a, b}. Also, demonstrate that your answer satisfies the pigeonhole principle by showing why it is not possible for all elements in B to have more than one preimage under any function from A to B. (i) Compute the total number of onto functions. (ii) Explain how the pigeonhole principle is relevant to this problem.

A class contains 10 boys and 20 girls. (i) In how many ways can a committee of 5 members be formed such that it includes at least one boy? (ii) How many different ways are there to select 4 letters from the word 'MATHEMATICS' without repetition, considering the repeated letters? Explain your answer.

Construct elementary proofs using ordinary induction to show that for all positive integers n, the sum of the first n odd numbers is equal to n². That is, prove Σ(2𝑖−1) = 𝑛² for 𝑖=1 to 𝑛.

Construct elementary proofs using ordinary induction to show that the sequence defined recursively by a_1 = 2 and a_{n+1} = 3a_n + 4 for all positive integers n, satisfies the explicit formula a_n = \frac{3^n + 1}{2}. Use this assumption to prove that a_{k+1} = \frac{3^{k+1} + 1}{2}. (iii) Discuss how strong induction could be used as an alternative method for proving the same result.
